scenes.narration: [serious] A computer virus secretly broke machines inside Iran's nuclear site.
The place was called Natanz. Inside, many machines spun very fast. They made nuclear fuel.
It probably came in on a USB stick. Then it found the boxes that run the machines.

visuals.title: How it got in
items: Came in on a USB stick

scenes.narration: Next, it made the machines spin at the wrong speed. But the screens still showed everything was fine.
Experts say Iran had to replace about 1,000 machines.
Then the virus escaped. It spread to computers around the world. Experts in Belarus were called to help.
Reports say America and Israel made it. Neither ever said yes. A computer virus had become a weapon.

facts.claim: Stuxnet was designed to arrive on a removable drive such as a USB stick, targeted specific Siemens PLCs controlling uranium-enrichment centrifuges, made them spin erratically while reporting normal readings to operators
Stuxnet came to light in 2010 after an office in Iran asked Belarusian Sergey Ulasen of antivirus firm VirusBlokAda for help with rebooting computers

ISIS (Institute for Science and International Security) reported that Iran replaced about 1,000 centrifuges at the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant in late 2009 or early 2010 and that Stuxnet is a reasonable explanation
The New York Times (2012) reported the operation 'Olympic Games', begun under Bush and accelerated under Obama; an element of it accidentally became public in summer 2010
It is widely believed that U.S. and Israeli intelligence created Stuxnet; neither government has officially acknowledged it

seo.title: Stuxnet: The Computer Worm That Broke Iran's Nuclear Machines
seo.description: Stuxnet was a hidden program that made Iran's uranium centrifuges spin wrong while screens showed all was normal. Reports say the U.S. and Israel built it, but neither has admitted it. Learn what the Stuxnet virus was and how it sabotaged Iran's nuclear program. #cybersecurity #stuxnet #cyberwar #shorts
